task-intent.statement: Execute a human ruling that the engine must permit the `start` its HARD advisory instructs.

expected-behavior.statement: The engine refuses that start, so the fix is to make it stop refusing.

observed-behavior.statement: Measured before changing anything: the engine does NOT refuse it. The advisory names an order ('First request a refresh; THEN begin'), and an agent obeying that order has a keyed request on file by the time it starts, which sends the guard down its release path -- the start is permitted. The predecessor's observed refusal came from starting BEFORE attaching, out of the advisory's stated order. What actually fires on perfect obedience is the trip ledger recording `begin-released` and the next `current` rendering the agent as an over-the-line offender.

impact-cost.statement: Implementing the ruling literally would have been a no-op: the lane would have reported success while the measured symptom survived untouched.

workaround.statement: Reproduce the reported symptom end-to-end at the real chokepoint before implementing a ruling about it, even when the ruling is settled and pasted verbatim into the order -- a settled decision can still rest on a misread mechanism.

task-intent.statement: Change the smallest engine behavior that stops the compliance ledger branding an agent for obeying the advisory.

expected-behavior.statement: The `begin-released` outcome is incidental to this one seam, so exempting the instructed start is a local change.

observed-behavior.statement: #467's central demonstration case WAS the engine-instructed case: four of its tests demonstrate `begin-released` using exactly `start` at a pending active gate with a request on file -- precisely the move #510's advisory later began instructing. The two issues had been contradicting each other since #510 shipped, with no state difference to tell the cases apart.

impact-cost.statement: The collision forced re-aiming five tests in a class the issue does not own, which is a much larger blast radius than a one-branch engine change suggests.

workaround.statement: When two issues disagree, check whether the older one's DEMONSTRATION fixture is the newer one's mandated behavior; if it is, re-aim the fixture onto a case that is still genuinely the agent's own choice rather than weakening the assertion.

task-intent.statement: Obey pre-ruling 3: enumerate every test asserting on the refusal or the trip ledger BEFORE changing behavior.

expected-behavior.statement: An enumeration would list the obvious anchor-class tests and cost time better spent implementing.

observed-behavior.statement: The enumeration predicted the collateral exactly: after the engine change the engine test file failed on precisely the six tests it named, five collateral plus the one pre-existing deliberate red. No surprises, and the trap that defeated the previous repair (a whole-string pin in a class named for a DIFFERENT issue, invisible to any targeted selector) was identified before it could fire.

impact-cost.statement: Converted what had been a wave-ending surprise into a planned edit list; the cost was one search pass.

workaround.statement: Enumerate the pinning tests before touching a shared rendered surface, and treat the enumeration's predicted failure set as the acceptance criterion for the change.

task-intent.statement: Get the engine change independently falsified before closing the lane.

expected-behavior.statement: An independent reviewer would re-run the tests and check the diff.

observed-behavior.statement: The falsifier built a 1152-state grid and ran two sweeps I had not thought of: a differential sweep proving zero states differ between old and new engine in raise/entry-count/gate-status (exactly 3 relabel), and an implication sweep proving every exempted state is one the advisory literally instructed. It also caught that I had told it the schema-doc staleness was 'floated to the Admiral' when it was on no durable record, and routed the float itself.

impact-cost.statement: The sweeps upgraded the narrowness claim from argued to measured, and the caught false claim would otherwise have left a real follow-up invisible to the Admiral.

workaround.statement: Give a falsifier the claims rather than the conclusion, and state which claims you are least sure of; and never describe a side effect as 'floated' unless it is on a durable record you can point at.

task-intent.statement: Record the run's findings at the path the frozen launch order names.

expected-behavior.statement: Writing .agent-work/epic-568-510/FINDINGS-wave2-engine.md would satisfy the order's Data Locations clause.

observed-behavior.statement: The harness refused the write with 'Subagents should return findings as text, not write report files', which directly collides with a frozen order that names that exact path. The separately mandated ENGINE_RESULT.md at the same directory wrote without objection.

impact-cost.statement: One mandated artifact could not be produced; its content had to be folded into the result document instead.

workaround.statement: Do not route around a tool-level guard with shell writes: fold the content into the artifact that is permitted and report the collision so the order or the guard can be reconciled by whoever owns them.

task-intent.statement: Drive this run's own spine to closeout through the engine.

expected-behavior.statement: The gauge would report this session's context honestly and the HARD band would not fire during mechanical closeout.

observed-behavior.statement: From `reconcile` onward the engine's own calibration for claude-opus-5 (soft 0.08 / hard 0.15) put a ~0.22 fill over the hard line, so every remaining gate required the documented release path -- attach a keyed refresh-request, then start -- even though the session's real remaining budget was very large and the remaining work was mechanical.

impact-cost.statement: Four closeout gates each needed a refresh-request that did not reflect genuine handoff intent, which pollutes the spine's evidence with requests a later reader could misread.

workaround.statement: Record the reason in the request's own note field at the moment of attaching it, and disclose the pattern in the result, so the records cannot be mistaken for a real handoff.

task-intent.statement: Add a wave-2 gate to the run's existing execute.json sub-checklist so the engine sees the new work.

expected-behavior.statement: The engine's `append` verb would add a gate to the completed gated sub-checklist.

observed-behavior.statement: REFUSED: 'append only on survey checklists'. A completed gated sub-checklist cannot take a new gate, so a second wave of work in the same lane has no place to live inside it.

impact-cost.statement: The wave-2 engine work is evidenced at the parent spine's reopened execute step instead of in the sub-checklist that tracked wave 1, so the two waves are recorded at different granularities.

workaround.statement: Evidence the later wave at the parent step it was reopened under, rather than fabricating sub-checklist structure the engine will not accept.

task-intent.statement: Interact with this run's spine through the MCP door, as prior orders required.

observed-behavior.statement: The door resolved to the interactive-demo scratch spine under the PRE-RELOCATION path constellation-skills-wt/f-424/, the third consecutive Commander in this lane to hit it. Separately, scripts/run_crew.py has since grown a --spine flag that binds SPINE_FILE into a spawned child's environment, so dispatched crews CAN get their own door -- the gap now only affects an agent whose door was bound by the harness before its process started.

impact-cost.statement: Every spine mutation went through the CLI fallback; provenance is identical but the mandated transport was unusable for a third run.

workaround.statement: Use the engine CLI with an explicit --session-id and say so plainly; the door is a transport, not a separate authority, and hand-editing spine state is the only thing the prohibition actually protects against.
